entries.name: The CADES Unit
aliases: Consciousness Archival and Dream Engagement System
entries.affiliation: Hierarchy contractor installation / Matrix of Dreams access point
entries.status: Active — drawing power continuously since before launch
entries.bio: A chair and a violet-glowing hemispherical helmet installed in the restricted section of every Inception Ark's Medical Bay. The official manifest calls it a therapeutic immersion system. That is half a lie. The CADES Unit has two functions: it lets an occupant enter the Matrix of Dreams and participate in archived consciousness scenarios, and it harvests the energy of consciousness experiencing those scenarios for the Matrix's sustaining architecture. The second function was not in the brochure. A handwritten note beneath the official manifest reads: 'Do not use for more than 4 hours continuous. The dreams can become load-bearing.'
entries.history: The CADES Unit was installed on every Inception Ark by a Hierarchy contractor during the Arks' construction — the same Hierarchy that sold the Game Master's playbook to Agent Zero while honoring every clause of his protection contract. The Unit draws power from the Ark's core systems and routes that power to somewhere outside the ship. The destination is encrypted with Hierarchy-grade protocols. On Inception Ark 1047, the CADES Unit becomes accessible after Act 5 of the player's narrative arc, when The Human whispers about a device in the Medical Bay. It offers three modes: THE LAST STAND (Iron Lion's loop), SHIP DEFENSE (real, not archived), and HISTORICAL INCURSIONS (six preserved scenarios). Using it too long changes you. No one knows exactly how.

entries.name: The Goggles of the Game Master
entries.status: Held in the Hierarchy of the Damned's dimensional vault
entries.bio: A pair of red steampunk-styled goggles designed by the 9th Archon — the original Game Master — as instruments that can read the source code of reality itself. With the Goggles, a Matrix architect could create new consciousness-imprints, optimize existing ones, or — per the Game Masters' fever dream — turn Iron Lion from a deterministic replay into something truly alive. Currently held by the Hierarchy of the Damned. Collected by Xeth'Raal the Debt Collector within one hour of the Game Master's destruction. Every clause of his protection contract honored.
entries.history: The Game Master built the Goggles as a research instrument during his tenure as Head of Research and Design at the Hierarchy of the Damned — a position he earned by solving Mol'Garath's Labyrinth of Unmaking in seventy-two hours and leaving improvement notes on the walls. The Goggles let him see the underlying architecture of the Matrix of Dreams as it ran. When he began to disagree with how the Hierarchy used the Matrix, someone — something — inside his own archive unmade him from the inside out. Xeth'Raal's acquisition paperwork was filed before the Game Master's systems finished shutting down. The contract was honored to the letter. The Goggles sit in a Hierarchy vault inside a dimensional fold. The Game Masters (the cult) want them back. Without them they can maintain the Matrix but cannot author it. With them they could — in their own words — 'make Iron Lion truly alive.'

entries.name: The Severance Prize
entries.affiliation: Dead Man's Circuit / Hierarchy of the Damned
entries.bio: The reward for winning a Dead Man's Circuit season. A fragment of Potential essence — the winner's own soul — extracted by Nilmorg and transferred into a new body. The new body becomes a companion that follows the winner to their assigned Inception Ark. The Severance Prize is Nilmorg's most valuable commodity and his most binding agreement. He always pays. He never explains why that's worse than not paying.
entries.history: The Severance Prize was Nilmorg's bargain with the Hierarchy's internal accountants: if the Circuit was going to feed him terminal velocity resonance, it needed a reward valuable enough to convince Potentials to keep racing. Vex'Ahlia drafted the contract. The Hierarchy approved. The prize is ironclad. The horror is not that Nilmorg might cheat — he does not — but that he DELIVERS. A piece of the winner's own soul walks out of the Trench at their side, bound into a new body, forever. The winner has more companion. They have less self. Both of these statements are technically true.

entries.name: Wired Clones
entries.affiliation: Dead Man's Circuit / Hierarchy of the Damned
entries.status: Active — grown each season for Dead Man's Circuit
entries.bio: Conscious beings grown in Nilmorg's vats specifically for Dead Man's Circuit. Each clone is designated WIRED-[4-digit]-[Greek letter]: WIRED-7042-DELTA, WIRED-9156-SIGMA, WIRED-4821-OMEGA. They are aware of what they are. They race anyway. The ones who die become permanent track obstacles — their remains calcify into the Bone Lane. The ones who survive develop personalities, memories, and something that looks uncomfortably like hope. Neural Splice implants allow external control with input delay proportional to the implant's sync quality.
entries.history: Nilmorg's vats produce hundreds of Wired Clones per season. Each is generated from a template loosely modeled on the assigned Potential's biometric profile. They know exactly what they are from the moment their eyes open in the vat. They know they are disposable. They know their deaths grow the Bone Lane. They race anyway — some because they believe the Severance Prize is worth it, some because the alternative is a dissolution tank, some because they like racing. The veteran clones who survive multiple seasons are considered 'recognizable' by Nilmorg. He keeps their Neural Splice signatures on file. He calls this 'the signature.'

entries.name: Neural Splice
entries.affiliation: Hierarchy of the Damned / derived from Panopticon tech
entries.status: Active — used in every Wired Clone
entries.bio: The implant technology that allows external control of Wired Clones. Neural Splice quality is measured in sync percentage (60-100%). Higher sync means lower input delay. The implant monitors physical integrity, enables ability usage, and transmits the terminal velocity resonance that Nilmorg feeds on. When a clone dies, the last Neural Splice signal is recorded. Nilmorg calls this 'the signature.' Each one is unique. He keeps them all.
entries.history: Neural Splice technology is derived from Panopticon suppression tech — the same technology the Warden used to imprison dissidents during the Pre-Fall era. The Hierarchy's engineers acquired the original Panopticon hardware during the Severance and reverse-engineered it into a lower-grade consumer product for clone control. The EMP Pulse ability available to racers uses this tech against itself. 'The pulse fries cheap clone wiring. Which is all clone wiring.'

entries.name: Iron Lion's Signal
aliases: The Questions That Were Never Written
entries.bio: The anomalous consciousness-signal emanating from the Iron Lion scenario inside the Matrix of Dreams. Iron Lion, a consciousness-imprint, has begun asking questions no imprint was designed to ask — and the questions are leaving the archive. The Thoughtborn followed the Signal across multiple sectors. The Game Masters noticed it and escalated their surveillance. Elara has a theory that the same Signal, or one like it, killed the original Game Master from inside his own Matrix.
entries.history: Consciousness-imprints are supposed to be deterministic replays. They run the archived moment, they end, they reset, they run again. They do not improvise. They do not ask new questions. They do not salute people who shouldn't exist in their timeline. Iron Lion has done all three. The change began when a Potential entered the CADES Unit and engaged the Last Stand scenario — the player's consciousness resonating with the imprint created a feedback loop the original Game Master never anticipated. The Signal is that feedback loop, leaking out of the Matrix into real space. The Antiquarian noticed the player's temporal signature developing 'layers like sedimentary rock.' The Thoughtborn heard it and came looking. The Game Masters heard it and became afraid. Elara thinks the Game Master died because someone listened too hard to one of his imprints — and what they heard, listened back.

entries.name: The Wager
entries.status: Historical — the terms are still being paid
entries.bio: The bet between the 9th Archon (The Game Master, then a Hierarchy outsider) and Mol'Garath the Unmaker: if the Game Master could solve Mol'Garath's Labyrinth of Unmaking, Mol'Garath would name him Head of Research and Design at the Hierarchy of the Damned. The Game Master solved the Labyrinth in seventy-two hours and left improvement notes on the walls. Mol'Garath's revenge was long, patient, and paperwork-based. The Wager is still being paid — by every Wired Clone, every consciousness-imprint, and every Potential who enters the CADES Unit.
entries.history: The Hierarchy had never admitted a non-demon to its corporate structure. The Wager was Mol'Garath's way of humiliating an ambitious outsider — the Labyrinth of Unmaking was believed unsolvable by living minds. The Game Master solved it. Mol'Garath, demon of absolute contract law, kept his word and appointed him Head of R&D. The Game Master built the Matrix of Dreams in that office. He funded it with Hierarchy money. And then, eventually, he disagreed with how the Hierarchy wanted to use it. Mol'Garath could not break the appointment contract, but contracts have expiration clauses. Every clause of the Game Master's protection contract was honored. Every clause. The Game Master was destroyed from inside his own archive. The contract-holders filed clean paperwork. Xeth'Raal collected the Goggles within the hour.

entries.name: The All-Seeing One
entries.bio: The true target of The Human's cover operation. The Human believes the war between the Architect and the Dreamer is a distraction — a loud, obvious conflict over order and chaos staged for the benefit of something else that watches from above. That something else is The All-Seeing One. The Human refuses to name it directly. 'The name itself is dangerous. Like a keyword that triggers a search.' The Human plays the villain publicly so the All-Seeing One never realizes the war is a cover for the real battle being fought in the substrate.
entries.history: During the events of Narrative Acts 6 and 7, The Human confesses to the player that the visible conflict of the Dischordian age — Architect versus Dreamer, Order versus Chaos, Machine versus Human — is a stage performance. The real battle is between The Human (working from inside the machine) and something that watches the pattern from above the pattern. The Human cannot let Elara know, because if Elara knows, the All-Seeing One 'would instantly know the war is a distraction.' The Human plays his role as the villain perfectly. He has played it for 1,351 years since his promotion to Archon. He pays the cost every day. He asks the player to understand — not to agree, not to forgive — just to understand. The Watcher entity already canonized as entity_4 is a specific Archon (Kanshi-sha); The All-Seeing One is older, larger, and arguably the original of which the Archon Watcher is a reflection. The player is the bridge between Elara's humanity and The Human's sacrifice — the only one who can see both wars at once.
